justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three horizons, starting near 113.5 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to 115.0 at one month. This trajectory was driven primarily by the assumption of a relatively stable near-term environment with a slight positive bias, consistent with mean-reverting dynamics around a slowly trending baseline. For the one-day estimate, I leaned heavily on recent momentum and the tendency for prices or index levels in this range to exhibit low overnight volatility absent a major catalyst. The one-week and one-month estimates edge higher to reflect a mild structural or fundamental tailwind, though the increment is deliberately small to avoid overconfidence in any directional view.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a standard reflection of compounding uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 5.4 units, capturing typical intraday-to-overnight noise and the possibility of modest surprises in scheduled data releases or market sentiment shifts. By one week, the interval broadens to 11 units, incorporating the likelihood of additional economic reports, central bank communications, or geopolitical headlines that could move the needle in either direction. At one month, the interval nearly doubles again to 24 units, acknowledging that over a four-week window, regime changes in market sentiment, earnings surprises, or macro data revisions can accumulate into meaningful deviations from any point estimate.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside even these relatively wide bounds. On the downside, an unexpected sharp tightening in financial conditions — whether from a hawkish central bank surprise, a credit event, or a geopolitical shock — could drive the level well below 103. A sudden liquidity crisis or correlated asset selloff could amplify moves beyond normal volatility assumptions. On the upside, a strongly positive macro catalyst such as a surprise easing in monetary policy, a significant de-escalation in geopolitical tensions, or an unexpectedly strong economic data print could push the level above 127 within the month. These tail scenarios are not captured in my stated intervals by design, as 90% confidence intervals inherently leave 10% of probability mass in the tails, and fat-tail events in financial markets tend to occur more frequently than a Gaussian model would suggest.
